title: Cope Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cope wells have a 60-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $8,100-$15,300.
h1: Cope, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Cope means evaluating a plains well, not just looking at a permit number. Records within five miles show 383 permitted wells, with 205 recorded as constructed. Of the wells reporting depth, the median is 60 feet, and reported yields are generally strong, although the available yield sample is limited to 36 wells.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records around Cope. Nearby places such as Joes, Kirk, Seibert, Vona, Flagler, and Stratton can provide broader context, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for a particular lot. Ground conditions, water rights, construction, and the location of the well on the property still matter.

sections.heading: Cope wells are usually shallow, but the ground still decides
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Cope is 60 feet. The middle half runs from 46 to 150 feet, so many drilling bids should be based on a relatively shallow hole, while still allowing for meaningful variation. About 69% of wells are under 100 feet, 30% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 1% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 450 feet.

These records name the Ogallala on 134 permits, the High Plains Aquifer on 10, and an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 237. Cope is not showing Denver Basin aquifer wells in this dataset. A driller should review nearby logs before pricing the job, because plains sediment and bedrock can change across a short distance.

sections.heading: Reported well yields around Cope are generally useful
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 25.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 15.0 to 500.0 gallons per minute. Among the 36 wells that report a pump yield, 81% are above 15 gallons per minute and 19% are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 5 gallons per minute in this dataset.

That is encouraging for a household, but it is not a promise for an untested lot. Yield figures may reflect different testing methods and uses, including domestic, stock, and irrigation wells. Ask for the well construction report and pumping information. A permitted exempt household-use well also has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, even if the aquifer could produce more.

sections.heading: Water levels near Cope are relatively close to the surface
sections.html:
Only 19 permits report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. Within that group, the median depth to static water is 33 feet, and the middle half runs from 22 to 112 feet. That suggests water is often encountered fairly shallowly in the reported wells, but it does not establish the water level for every parcel.

The permit history does not provide a water-level series by decade, so these facts do not show a defensible long-term rise or decline. Before buying, compare nearby well logs and ask for current information from the seller or driller. Static level, pumping level, seasonal conditions, and well location can all affect what a new pump system needs.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long-running drilling around Cope
sections.html:
Cope has a long record of well construction, with permits issued from the 1950s through the 2020s. The records show 23 permits in the 1950s, 23 in the 1960s, 43 in the 1970s, 18 in the 1980s, 27 in the 1990s, 35 in the 2000s, 17 in the 2010s, and 11 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Klassen Drilling, also recorded as Klassen, Paul C, with 56 permits; Schaal Drilling Co., also recorded as Schaal, Ruben T., with 24; and Wrape & Payne with 20. Older records may not reflect current availability or pricing. Use the names as a starting point, then verify licensing, insurance, scope, and who will complete the pump and electrical work.

sections.heading: A median-depth Cope well pencils out at $8,100-$15,300 finished
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at about $2,100-$3,300. That is not the project total.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,100-$15,300. A bid can move outside that range if the hole is deeper than expected, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the electrical and trench route is more involved. Request a written breakdown that separates drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic spacing, and the building plan
sections.html:
The mapped environmental record within about 10 miles includes 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site. There are 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped facts. That does not make untreated well water automatically safe. Test a private well for the contaminants relevant to the site and proposed use, and retest after construction or any change in taste, odor, or appearance.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where nearby wells perform well. Confirm that the proposed well location works with the septic system, replacement area, driveway, utility trench, and house foundation. Colorado permits, water rights, and augmentation requirements can affect what a well may legally supply, particularly in an over-appropriated basin. Have the site reviewed before closing or excavating.

sections.heading: For a Cope lot, buy the records before you buy the dirt
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and nearby wells. Look for total depth, casing and grout details, aquifer description, static level, pump yield, and the permitted use. The local records include domestic or household, stock, and irrigation wells, so a nearby irrigation result should not be treated as a direct household forecast.

For a new build, get a driller to inspect access and propose a well location before finalizing the house site. Carry a realistic allowance for the complete system, not just the hole. Confirm septic feasibility, electrical service, water testing, and the legal use of the well. A well inspection and a written drilling estimate are small steps compared with discovering after purchase that the lot cannot support the intended home.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cope, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Cope is 60 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 46 to 150 feet. About 69% are under 100 feet, while the deepest recorded well is 450 feet. A nearby log is useful for planning, but it cannot guarantee the depth on a particular parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cope?
faq.a: The local model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,100-$3,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,100-$15,300. Access, depth, casing, grout, trench length, and electrical work can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Cope wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 36 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 25.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 500.0 gallons per minute. Reported yields are not a guarantee for a new well, and testing methods and well uses vary. Review the construction report and pumping information before relying on a neighboring result.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Cope, Colorado?
faq.a: The mapped area has 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 0 historic mine features. Those facts do not establish water quality at a specific home. Test the private well for relevant contaminants, especially after construction, a property transfer, or any change in taste, odor, or appearance.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Cope?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction report, depth, static water level, yield, casing, grout, and permitted use. The local median depth is 60 feet and the median reported yield is 25.0 gallons per minute, but only 19 permits report static level and 36 report yield. Also confirm septic feasibility, legal water use, access, utilities, and the cost of a complete system.
